title: "SAF in Brief"
---

*The Statistical Architecture Framework in ten minutes: what it is, the two ideas at its core, what it gives you, and what it asks of you.*

::: {.callout-tip title="Who this is for"}
Anyone deciding whether their office should engage with SAF, and where: CIOs and CTOs, architects, methodologists and statisticians, quality and privacy officers, programme managers. **No architecture background is assumed** — where a word is used in a special sense, the [Glossary](glossary.qmd) explains it.

It is a ten-minute read. It summarises the [SAF Framework document](framework/index.qmd); it does not replace it. If you want to try SAF on one of your own statistical products, continue with [Getting Started with SAF](SAF-Getting-Started.qmd).
:::

## Why SAF

Statistical organisations share a need: production must remain credible, secure, and efficient while adapting to new data sources, new user expectations, and tighter constraints. The Statistical Architecture Framework (SAF) gives national statistical offices (NSOs) a common architectural foundation for making those changes in a controlled and coherent way.

SAF improves on the Common Statistical Production Architecture (CSPA) and the Common Statistical Data Architecture (CSDA). It keeps their ambition — shared understanding across organisations, interoperability, reuse, standardised building blocks — but shifts the centre of gravity from describing to doing. It is meant to be used directly in programmes and projects, to guide real design and implementation choices.

It does not compete with the standards an office already uses. GSBPM, GAMSO and GSIM stay exactly where they are. SAF supplies the connecting tissue between them: the link from strategy, through capabilities and processes, to services and technology.

::: {.callout-important title="A mapping framework, not an operating model"}
"SAF does not prescribe a single operating model, a single technology stack, or a single organisational design. It recognises that NSOs differ in mandate, maturity, and context. Instead, it provides a shared architectural foundation that can be adapted to local realities while remaining comparable across organisations." — *SAF Framework, [Definition of Scope](framework/introduction.qmd#definition-of-scope)*
:::

## The two ideas at its core

Much of SAF (*the motivation layer, the GAMSO-derived capability model, the ten value streams*) will look familiar to anyone who knows the UNECE standards. Two ideas are SAF's own, and everything about *applying* the framework hangs off them.

### Steady states of data

Statistical production is split into six stages, called **value streams** and numbered VS-01 to VS-06. Each adds one particular kind of value to the data, and each works independently of the others — *loosely coupled*, in architecture terms.

They exchange data only at defined points called **steady states**. A steady state is a dataset finished to a known quality, given a version and an identifier, and made available for the next stage to pick up. One stream produces it, the next consumes it, and neither needs to know anything about how the other works inside.

The handover is announced, not assumed. When a stream finishes a dataset it **registers** it — records it in a catalogue with its identifier and a description of what was done to it — and that registration sends an event telling the next stream new data is ready.

::: {.callout-note title="\"Registered\" does not mean a statistical register"}
In the context of SAF, *registering* a dataset means cataloguing it so others can find and cite the exact version. It has nothing to do with a statistical register such as the business register or the population register. Both meanings appear in these documents; the [Glossary](glossary.qmd) keeps them apart.
:::

| State | Name | Produced by | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| (#0) | Source Data | *external providers* | Data at the external holder, before it enters the NSO (pre-ingestion; not a numbered SAF state) |
| #1 | Raw Data | VS-01 | Received into NSO custody in original form, with its provenance — where it came from and how — and basic validation |
| #2 | Standardized Data | VS-02 | Aligned to common structure, format, and classifications — **values unchanged** |
| #3 | Processed Data | VS-03 | Content validated, edited, imputed, enriched, integrated; derived variables added |
| #4 | Statistics (Output Data) | VS-04 → VS-05 | Estimated/aggregated statistics (VS-04), composed into approved products (VS-05) |
| #5 | Released Data | VS-06 | Disclosure-controlled, documented, published or delivered to external parties |
| #6 | Consumed Data | *external users* | Data in use outside the NSO's direct control |

### The four-process governance pattern

Every stream is described through the same **four process types**. This is not a one-off sequence but a repeating cycle, and each of the four produces a distinct kind of result:

- **Design** — decide how the work should be done: rules, methodology, specifications, policies. *Provides metadata.*
- **Implementation** — build, configure, and test the systems that will do it. *Provides the execution process.*
- **Execution** — run the work each production cycle. *Provides the statistical data.*
- **Management** — check quality, monitor performance, and feed improvements back to Design. *Provides quality reports.*

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-brief-cycle
%%| fig-cap: "The four-process governance pattern. Each of the six primary streams runs this full cycle; the feedback arrow from Management to Design closes the loop."
%%| fig-width: 6
flowchart LR
    D["**Design**
    _metadata_"] -->|"guides building"| I["**Implement**
    _execution process_"]
    I -->|"production-ready"| E["**Execute**
    _statistical data_"]
    E -->|"data & process logs"| M["**Manage**
    _quality reports_"]
    M -->|"improvement feedback"| D

    style D fill:#7c3aed,color:#fff,stroke:#6d28d9
    style I fill:#2563eb,color:#fff,stroke:#1d4ed8
    style E fill:#059669,color:#fff,stroke:#047857
    style M fill:#d97706,color:#fff,stroke:#b45309
```


::: {.callout-tip title="For GSBPM readers"}

Design maps to Phase 2, Implementation to Phase 3, Execution to Phases 4–7 as appropriate to the domain, and Management to the overarching Quality Management / Phase 8. Separating the four lets an office change how a stream is *built* without touching how it is *designed*, and govern quality without owning execution.

:::


## How the pieces fit

Six primary streams form the production chain. Four **supporting** streams (VS-07 Governance & Compliance, VS-08 Innovation & Methodological Development, VS-09 Infrastructure & Platform Enablement, VS-10 Customer & Stakeholder Engagement) enable and constrain all six continuously. They have no steady-state transition, run as a plan → build → operate → improve cycle, produce enabling capabilities rather than data, and align to GAMSO rather than GSBPM.

| VS | Domain | State in → out | Signature discipline |
|---|---|---|---|
| **01** | Acquisition & Ingestion | Source → #1 Raw | Metadata & validation at ingestion |
| **02** | Standardization & Integration | #1 → #2 Standardized | No loss of content — map, coerce, annotate |
| **03** | Editing & Enrichment | #2 → #3 Processed | Full traceability of every value change |
| **04** | Estimation & Modeling | #3 → #4 Statistics | Methodological transparency + accuracy + initial disclosure control |
| **05** | Product Composition | within #4 (→ approved) | Coherence & interpretability; approval before registration |
| **06** | Dissemination & Service Delivery | #4 → #5 Released → #6 | Accessibility & trust; final disclosure-control gate |
: The six primary value streams {tbl-colwidths="[8,30,24,38]"}

The last column of that table names each stream's **signature discipline**: the one rule that defines it — what it must always do, and what it must never do.

Beneath the streams sit the **capability model** (70 capabilities in four groups, sourced from GAMSO 1.2) and the **motivation layer** (drivers, goals, principles, outcomes, stakeholders) — the framework's vocabulary and justification. The streams and steady states are where it is applied.

## What adopting SAF gives you

The framework names six outcomes for an office that adopts it: **accelerated modernization**, **enhanced data quality**, **improved interoperability**, **improved trust and transparency**, **increased efficiency**, and a **shared knowledge base** for the organizations and its partners.

In practice those follow from the steady states:

* State #2 puts data from different sources into common formats and classifications, so datasets can be combined and reused across products.
* State #3 is designed for reuse, so processing effort is not repeated unit by unit. Loose coupling means one capability — a collection channel, an editing engine, a dissemination platform — can be modernised without disrupting the chain. And because every dataset carries its **lineage** — the trace back through every step to the data it came from — together with its quality documentation, an office can show exactly how any published figure was produced.

For NSOs this means reduced risk, greater agility, and better alignment between IT and business objectives. For international organisations it means harmonisation and comparability. For citizens and policymakers it means statistics whose trustworthiness can be proven.

## What it commits you to

The benefits are not free. Adopting the steady-state model is a set of concrete obligations — this is what makes the loose coupling real rather than a diagram.

::: {.callout-important title="Adopting SAF means you commit to"}
- **Naming what is handed over at every boundary.** Streams exchange finished, registered datasets — *artefacts*, in SAF's vocabulary — together with their metadata, never internal working data. Neither side then needs to know how the other works inside (SAF-P07).
- **A catalogue.** Every artefact is identified, versioned and catalogued; once registered it is available to all authorised colleagues, so collection, cleaning and analysis are not duplicated across teams (SAF-P08).
- **Metadata everywhere.** Every artefact carries its provenance, method, accuracy, classification and lineage — captured at the moment each value is created or changed, not reconstructed months later (SAF-P09).
- **An owner and quality criteria per state.** Someone is accountable for each state, and a dataset must meet explicit criteria to *be* in that state.
- **Security built in.** Access control, integrity verification, and tamper-evident audit trails are embedded in every pipeline from the start (SAF-P10).
- **Confidentiality applied progressively.** Identifiers are removed or pseudonymised at standardisation (#2), disclosure risk is assessed on enrichment (#3), initial disclosure control is applied to outputs (#4), and a final disclosure-control gate stands before release (#5) — nothing proceeds if it fails (SAF-P11).
- **Design and management artefacts, not just execution.** Rules, methods, and specifications exist and are versioned before a cycle runs; quality reports and improvement recommendations feed back into design after it.
- **Events, not assumptions.** A handover is announced by a registration event; the next stream does not have to ask.
- **Open tooling where it carries statistical method.** Methods that produce official figures are built on shared, open components and contributed back, so the statistical community keeps collective control of them rather than depending on a vendor (SAF-P01). See [Open Source in SAF](open-source.qmd).
:::

One word behind all of this: artefacts are **immutable** — frozen once registered. A correction does not overwrite a registered dataset, it produces a new version. That is what makes it possible to point at a published figure years later and show precisely the data behind it.

None of these is prescriptive about *how* you meet it. A boundary is a contract, not an organisational unit: one team may own several states, and a central unit may run processing for many domains. What SAF fixes is that the contract exists and is explicit.

## Reading paths by role

The SAF Framework document is long. Start where your role needs to.

| Role | Start here | Then |
|---|---|---|
| Enterprise and data architects | [Architecture Principles](framework/motivation.qmd#architecture-principles); [Steady States of Data](framework/business-architecture.qmd#steady-states-of-data); [Principles to Apply](framework/business-architecture.qmd#principles-to-apply) | [Capability Model](framework/strategy.qmd#capability-model); the *Boundary Interface Specifications* in each VS deep dive |
| IT architects and delivery teams | [The Four-Process Governance Pattern](framework/business-architecture.qmd#the-four-process-governance-pattern); [VS-09 Infrastructure and Platform Enablement](framework/vs-09.qmd) | The *Implementation Processes* and *Business Services and Interfaces* sections of the stream you build for; the *Framework Mappings* tables |
| Methodologists | The *Steady State Transition* section of VS-02 to VS-05; the VS-03 and VS-04 *Signature discipline* notes in [The Statistical Data Value Chain](framework/business-architecture.qmd#the-statistical-data-value-chain) | The *Design Processes* of VS-02 to VS-05; [VS-08 Innovation and Methodological Development](framework/vs-08.qmd) |
| CIOs, CTOs, managers, policy makers | [Preface](framework/introduction.qmd#preface) and [Purpose](framework/introduction.qmd#purpose); [Motivation](framework/motivation.qmd#motivation) — drivers, goals, outcomes | [The Value Chain at a Glance](framework/business-architecture.qmd#the-value-chain-at-a-glance); the *Maturity Assessment Checklist* of any stream |
| Privacy officers and assurance functions | [SAF-P09](framework/motivation.qmd#saf-p09-no-data-without-metadata-and-classification), [SAF-P10](framework/motivation.qmd#saf-p10-security-by-design), [SAF-P11](framework/motivation.qmd#saf-p11-privacy-by-design); the *Two cross-chain disciplines* note under [Principles to Apply](framework/business-architecture.qmd#principles-to-apply) | The quality requirements of [State #2](framework/business-architecture.qmd#state-2-standardized-data) and [State #5](framework/business-architecture.qmd#state-5-published-output-data-released-data); [VS-07 Governance and Compliance](framework/vs-07.qmd); the *Required Metadata* column of every boundary specification |
